k-accomplished.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>sheep</radical> is being driven up a track: the <radical>road</radical> sweeps in underneath it, the surface <radical>splits</radical> into ruts, and packed <radical>earth</radical> climbs the whole way up. It is a long haul and the flock keeps stopping dead. But the last one is over the top and into the pen, and the job is <radical>accomplished</radical>.
k-accomplished.reading_mnemonic: Tatsu is the drover who marks the top of every hill the same way: one slap on the gatepost and a barked 「<reading>たつ</reading>」 — done, next. He has said it at every gate between here and the coast. たつ means it is finished.

k-ancestor.meaning_mnemonic: An <radical>altar</radical> stands on the left, and stacked on the right is an <radical>eye</radical> laid flat above a line of <radical>ground</radical> — a portrait propped up over the offerings, watching the room. Somebody long dead is looking back at you off that shelf. You bow to the face because it is your <radical>ancestor</radical>.
k-ancestor.reading_mnemonic: So is the small catch of sound the incense makes when it takes light at the altar — 「<reading>そ</reading>」 — and for a second the eye in the portrait seems to move. One syllable, once a year, for the ancestor. そ.

k-breath.meaning_mnemonic: Your own <radical>self</radical> sits on top — that nose you point at when you mean you — and directly underneath it, your <radical>heart</radical>. Nose above, heart below, and running between the two of them all day long is the one thing you never have to decide to do. In through the nose, down to the heart, back out: <radical>breath</radical>.
k-breath.reading_mnemonic: Soku is the swimmer who comes up after far too long under and takes one enormous ragged gulp — 「<reading>そく</reading>」 — nose first, heart going like a hammer. That is what a breath you badly needed sounds like. そく.

k-daughter.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>woman</radical> at the left, and beside her the whole shape of <radical>stopping</radical>: the eye that has seen something and the foot that will not take another step. She is planted in the doorway with her arms folded, and the young one is not going out tonight. A girl who gets stopped at the door is somebody's <radical>daughter</radical>.
k-daughter.reading_mnemonic: Jou is how the neighbours refer to her, drawn out and a shade too formal — 「<reading>じょう</reading>」 — the sort of address you use for a girl of good family who is very definitely not allowed out. She hears じょう and rolls her eyes.

k-daytime.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>body</radical> is slumped across the top with a single <radical>drop</radical> of sweat coming off it, and directly underneath sits the <radical>sun</radical>, pinned against a flat line of <radical>ground</radical>. It is straight overhead and there is no shade left anywhere. Work has stopped and everyone has lain down. This is the flattening middle of the <radical>daytime</radical>.
k-daytime.reading_mnemonic: Chuu the loyal mouse will not nap through it. While every other body is flat out he stands at his post in the full sun, squeaking 「<reading>ちゅう</reading>」 on the hour so that nobody oversleeps. Absurdly devoted, ちゅう, right through the worst of it.

k-doctor.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>box on its side</radical>, its open mouth turned towards you, and lying inside it an <radical>arrow</radical> — the one they have just drawn out of you, dropped in the tray. The lid comes down over the arrowhead and the wound both. Whoever owns that box and knows what to do with what comes out of you is the <radical>doctor</radical>.
k-doctor.reading_mnemonic: Ii is the noise she makes while examining you: one short noncommittal 「<reading>い</reading>」 as she looks at the wound, and another as she drops the arrow into the tray. Nothing whatsoever about い tells you whether it is bad news.

k-end.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the <radical>tree</radical>: a <radical>stick</radical> straight up the middle, branches <radical>split</radical> away either side, and laid across the very top an extra <radical>lid</radical> of a stroke, drawn longer than the <radical>one</radical> below it. That top bar marks the last inch of the highest twig — as far up as this tree is ever going to go. The tip is the <radical>end</radical>.
k-end.reading_mnemonic: Matsu is the woodsman who only ever takes the tip. He climbs the whole tree, snips the last bud off the top of it, and calls down 「<reading>まつ</reading>」 to say he has got there. まつ means there is nothing above him.

k-evening.meaning_mnemonic: Three strokes and nothing else: a curve like the shoulder of a hill, with one line falling through it. It is the moon, only half up and not yet bright, caught at the exact moment the light goes flat and blue and everything loses its edges. Nothing has happened yet. The whole character is one picture of <radical>evening</radical> starting.
k-evening.reading_mnemonic: Seki comes out onto his step at this hour every night, and you hear him before you see him — that wet, rattling 「<reading>せき</reading>」 of a cough carrying right down the street. When せき starts up, the light has gone.

k-father.meaning_mnemonic: Two arms crossing over each other at the top, two legs braced wide underneath. It is a stance, not a face — the shape of a man standing square in a doorway with his arms folded, filling the whole frame, waiting to hear what you have got to say for yourself. Everybody recognises that silhouette: <radical>father</radical>.
k-father.reading_mnemonic: Fu is the long breath out through the nose that he gives you instead of an answer — 「<reading>ふ</reading>」 — arms still folded. Not angry. Not pleased either. Just ふ, and you will be hearing it for the rest of your life.

k-friend.meaning_mnemonic: One stroke <radical>slides</radical> down from the top left across a bar of <radical>ground</radical>, and underneath it a <radical>right hand</radical> comes up to meet it. Two hands reaching in from opposite directions and closing on each other. Nobody is being paid for this and nobody is in charge of anybody. That is a <radical>friend</radical>.
k-friend.reading_mnemonic: Yuu is the one who is always there before you, hand already out, drawing the greeting into a long two-beat call across the car park — 「<reading>ゆう</reading>」 — before you have even shut the car door. ゆう means somebody is glad to see you.

k-gone.meaning_mnemonic: A mound of <radical>earth</radical> on top, and underneath it that little sealed <radical>cocoon</radical>, tucked well out of sight. Whatever was inside wrapped itself up, went under the soil, and never came back out. You can dig the whole mound over and there is nothing left in there to find. It is <radical>gone</radical>.
k-gone.reading_mnemonic: Kyo is the magician who buries things and cannot get them back. He taps the mound, says 「<reading>きょ</reading>」 with a flourish, and that is genuinely the end of the trick. No reappearance, no second half. きょ, and it is gone.

k-he.meaning_mnemonic: A single <radical>step</radical> at the left edge, and beside it a hide being hauled off in one sheet — all <radical>skin</radical>, no animal left. Someone walked past carrying it a moment ago and is already down the road. You never saw the face, only the back of him. That man over there, the one you point at and cannot name: <radical>he</radical>.
k-he.reading_mnemonic: Hii is the little intake of breath you make when the man in the skin cloak goes past without a word — 「<reading>ひ</reading>」 — and by the time you have finished it he is round the corner. Every single time you catch sight of him: ひ.

k-heart.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>wide box</radical> of a room, and shoved right to the back of it a store of <radical>rice</radical> with something <radical>big</radical> planted on top of the pile. You have to walk through every other room in the house to reach it, and nobody outside the family ever does. The deepest room is the building's <radical>heart</radical>.
k-heart.reading_mnemonic: Ou is the grandmother who lives in that back room and has not come out in years. Knock and you get one long syllable through the paper door — 「<reading>おう</reading>」 — meaning she heard you and no, you may not come in. おう, from the very back of the house.

k-husband.meaning_mnemonic: Take the <radical>big</radical> figure — the <radical>person</radical> standing with both arms flung out wide — and lay one more bar across the top of it like a <radical>lid</radical>, so there are <radical>two</radical> horizontal strokes up there instead of one. That extra line is the pin through his topknot. He is grown, he is married, and he would like you to notice: <radical>husband</radical>.
k-husband.reading_mnemonic: Fu is the same breath out through the nose you learned from his father, inherited exactly — arms folded in the doorway, one 「<reading>ふ</reading>」, no further comment offered. Getting married did not change it in the slightest.

k-me.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> stands at the far left, and stacked up beside him is a <radical>big</radical> load: a <radical>sheep</radical> he has to carry in, then <radical>split</radical> into portions for everyone else before he takes any himself. He does the hauling and he eats last, and when he speaks he uses the humble word for <radical>me</radical>.
k-me.reading_mnemonic: Boku is the errand boy who answers every question about who did it with the same word: 「<reading>ぼく</reading>」. Broke the gate? ぼく. Carried the sheep up the hill? ぼく. He never says his own name, so ぼく is the only name you have for him.

k-mister.meaning_mnemonic: Someone has swept the whole yard with a <radical>broom</radical>, one stroke that <radical>slides</radical> away to the left, until the <radical>ground</radical> is spotless. Then he opens his <radical>mouth</radical> and gives out tomorrow's orders. He is not the emperor, only the man directly above you — the <radical>mister</radical> whose name gets attached to every younger man in the room.
k-mister.reading_mnemonic: Kun is the teacher who refuses to use first names. Every boy in the class gets the same syllable barked after his surname — 「<reading>くん</reading>」 — as the seating chart comes out. Tanaka-くん. Sato-くん. It is how you know he means you.

k-morning.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> is caught low in a <radical>cross</radical>-braced frame on the left, still climbing, while over on the right the <radical>moon</radical> has not gone down yet. Both of them are up there at once. That happens for about twenty minutes a day, and only ever at one end of it: <radical>morning</radical>.
k-morning.reading_mnemonic: Chou is the long-distance runner who is out before anybody else, and she stretches her greeting the whole length of the street as she passes your window — a long, unreasonably cheerful 「<reading>ちょう</reading>」. If you hear ちょう, the moon is still up.

k-mother.meaning_mnemonic: A figure kneeling with her arms wrapped round in front of her, and two dots marking the breasts that fed you. The entire character is built around those two points; take them out and it turns into a different word altogether. They are the reason the shape exists at all, and the reason you call her <radical>mother</radical>.
k-mother.reading_mnemonic: Bo is the one syllable a baby manages long before it manages anything else — 「<reading>ぼ</reading>」 — blown out with a bubble of spit and aimed straight at whoever is holding it. She answers to ぼ years before she answers to her own name.

k-night.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>lid</radical> is pulled across the top of the sky, and a <radical>person</radical> slips underneath it just as the last of the <radical>evening</radical> drains away. Once that lid is on, nothing more gets in — no sun, no colour, nobody else. The lid down over the evening, with somebody still out under it: <radical>night</radical>.
k-night.reading_mnemonic: Ya is the yakitori man who only opens once the lid is down. The cart comes out of nowhere, the lantern goes up, and he calls one syllable into the dark — 「<reading>や</reading>」 — which is the entire advertisement. If you can hear や, it is night.

k-nightfall.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> on the left has finally been let off: the shape on the right is the one that squeezes out from under the heavy lid and walks away <radical>exempt</radical>. Its shift is done, it has clocked out, and it drops below the roofline without waiting to be dismissed. The sun excused from duty is <radical>nightfall</radical>.
k-nightfall.reading_mnemonic: Ban is the night watchman who takes over the moment the sun clocks off. He drags the gate shut and announces himself to the empty street — 「<reading>ばん</reading>」 — one flat syllable, every night, so you know the day is closed.

k-on-foot.meaning_mnemonic: A single <radical>step</radical> at the left edge, and beside it the entire shape of a <radical>run</radical> — thigh forward, foot planting, ground coming loose behind. Except there is no horse here, no cart, and no road worth the name. Whatever is getting done today is getting done <radical>on foot</radical>.
k-on-foot.reading_mnemonic: Toto the door-to-door turtle has never once taken a ride. He carries the sample doors on his shell and walks the entire round, and he announces himself at every house with the same syllable before he knocks — 「<reading>と</reading>」. と, and another mile.

k-private.meaning_mnemonic: A stalk of <radical>grain</radical> leans over on the left, and tucked in behind it on the right is a little <radical>cocoon</radical>, sealed tight. Nobody else knows it is there. You grew the whole crop out in the open, then wrapped one seed away for yourself and told no one. Grain kept back inside a cocoon is what is <radical>private</radical>.
k-private.reading_mnemonic: Shi is the quiet one who keeps her own small field behind the house, and when anyone asks what she is growing in it she says 「<reading>し</reading>」 and closes the gate. Not rude, exactly. Whatever is in there is hers, and し is the only answer you are ever going to get.

k-second-1.meaning_mnemonic: A stalk of <radical>grain</radical> on the left, and beside it the <radical>small</radical> mark. Not the ear, not the stalk — one single bristle off the very top of the head, the thinnest thing on the entire plant. Slice up an hour the same way and the sliver you are left holding is one <radical>second</radical>.
k-second-1.reading_mnemonic: Byou is the hospital timekeeper with the stopwatch, and she counts out loud in a flat clipped bark — 「<reading>びょう</reading>」, びょう, びょう — one for every tick. She will not speed up and she will not stop. びょう is a single second landing.

k-submit.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> on the left, and on the right <radical>two</radical> bars stacked over a line of <radical>ground</radical>, carried on a <radical>stick</radical> each and <radical>split</radical> apart at the foot into a pair of legs. It is a tray on a stand, lifted with both hands. He is not setting it down — he is holding it up for somebody above him to take, which is what it is to <radical>submit</radical> a thing.
k-submit.reading_mnemonic: Kyou is the offering-bearer who never lowers the tray. He walks the entire length of the hall with it over his head, announcing himself at every pillar — 「<reading>きょう</reading>」 — until somebody finally takes the weight off him.

k-uncle.meaning_mnemonic: A stick of <radical>divination</radical> up in the corner, a <radical>small</radical> mark beside it, and a <radical>right hand</radical> reaching in underneath to scoop the pair of them up. This is the younger brother: not the head of the family, so he gets the fortune-telling twigs and the small share, and he turns up at New Year to read your future for a laugh. Your <radical>uncle</radical>.
k-uncle.reading_mnemonic: Shuku is that uncle, and he arrives every year with the same trick. He shuffles the sticks, throws them down, sucks his teeth, and pronounces 「<reading>しゅく</reading>」 as though it settles the matter. Nobody knows what しゅく means. He will not explain.

k-what.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> stands at the left with a line in his hand — you can see the <radical>barb</radical> at the end of it, and a flat bar of <radical>ground</radical> above the open <radical>mouth</radical> below. He has hooked something out of the water and hauled it up, and now he is just staring at it with his mouth hanging open, because he has no idea <radical>what</radical> it is.
k-what.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the fire-breathing crow drops onto the power line above him and looks at the thing on the hook. She has never seen one either. All she manages is one puzzled croak — 「<reading>か</reading>?」 — with a little puff of flame behind it. か? か? Neither of them knows.

k-who.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Words</radical> stand on the left, and on the right an <radical>old bird</radical> with its head cocked, waiting. You have been talking for ten minutes and the bird still cannot work out which person you mean. It hops in closer and asks the only question you have left it: <radical>who</radical>?
k-who.reading_mnemonic: Sui is the owl who works the gate. She leans down, blinks once, and hoots 「<reading>すい</reading>」, which in owl means name, please. Nobody gets past her without answering it. すい, すい, until you say who you are.

k-wife.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>woman</radical> at the bottom, and above her a <radical>broom</radical> held up on its <radical>stick</radical>, with a bar of <radical>ground</radical> ruled straight across the top. She is not sweeping out somebody else's household here. The broom, the floor and the roofline over both are hers, and the person who runs them is the <radical>wife</radical>.
k-wife.reading_mnemonic: Sai is the one who actually decides. Ask her husband anything and he glances sideways at her first; she gives one flat 「<reading>さい</reading>」 and that is the answer on behalf of both of them. さい settles it.

k-yesterday.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> on the left, and on the right a <radical>stick</radical> driven upright into the dirt with one stroke that <radical>slides</radical> off it. That stick is a sundial, and the shadow it threw is still scratched into the ground beside it. The sun has moved on. The mark it left behind belongs to <radical>yesterday</radical>.
k-yesterday.reading_mnemonic: Saku is the old gardener who checks his shadow-stick every dawn and then grumbles about how much better the light was 「<reading>さく</reading>」 — his one-word shorthand for the day before. Nothing is ever as good as さく was.

k-zero.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Rain</radical> across the whole top of the character, and underneath it a <radical>person</radical> kneeling on the bare <radical>ground</radical> while the clerk presses her <radical>stamp</radical> down onto the ledger. It lands in the column where this year's crop should have been counted, and what it prints there is one perfect round <radical>zero</radical>. The rain took the lot.
k-zero.reading_mnemonic: Rei is that clerk. She is scrupulously polite about it — a small bow, a murmured 「<reading>れい</reading>」 — and then she inks the nothing into your row and moves down the line. れい, bow, zero. She has done it forty times today.
